note: The most famous nonsense in the poem. No one knows what it means, or whether it means anything. It sounds like a cry of alarm or an appeal to Satan. Early commentators heard a Latin exclamation of surprise in "pape" and the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet in "aleppe". Virgil, at least, seems to understand it.

context: He was named in the last line of Canto 6. Dante gives him a swollen face, a wolf's nature and a voice that can't form real words.
The wolf is Dante's animal for greed. Calling Plutus one ties the guardian of this circle to the beast of Canto 1.
The "proud rebellion" is that of Lucifer and his angels, the first sin of all. Virgil reminds one of the losers of that war whose side he is on.

note: All bluster and nothing behind it. Plutus is puffed up like the wealth he stands for, and collapses at a word.
The circle of the misers and the spendthrifts, punished together.
The whirlpool of ancient legend in the Strait of Messina, between Sicily and the Italian mainland, where currents from two seas meet and break against each other.
Dante's word names a round dance of his day, in which the dancers circled and turned back. A bitter joke: this dance is done with boulders.

The punishment fits the sin. They gave their lives to dead matter, piling it up or throwing it away, and now they heave dead weight around forever to no purpose. The two crowds push in opposite directions round the circle and collide. The image recalls Sisyphus, who in Greek myth rolls a rock uphill forever.
Each crowd shouts the other's sin at it. Misers and spendthrifts despise each other, and neither can see that they failed in the same way.
The tonsure: clergy shaved the crown of the head as the sign of their calling. The crowd on the left are the misers.
The idea comes from Aristotle's Ethics: a virtue is the right measure between two extremes. The right use of money lies between hoarding and squandering, and both crowds missed it.
The poem's first open attack on the greed of the Church, one of its great themes. Dante names no one here. He will name popes in Inferno 19.
In life they could not tell what was worth having. Now no one can tell them apart. As with the neutrals of Canto 3, Dante names nobody in this circle.
At the resurrection the misers will rise tight-fisted and the spendthrifts with cropped hair. An Italian saying has the wasteful man spend everything, down to the hair on his head.
Heaven.
Dante's phrase is "the short buffa", a word that can mean a jest or a puff of wind. Either way, worldly wealth is a brief trick and then gone.

context: Virgil mentions her in passing, and Dante's question draws out a full account of who she is. It is one of the first passages of pure teaching in the poem.

note: On earth. Everything below the sphere of the moon, the lowest of the heavens, belonged to the world of change and decay. Above it nothing altered.

quote: He whose wisdom transcends all things
note: God.

The angels. In Dante's universe each of the heavenly spheres is turned by an order of angels, called intelligences. Fortune is one more of them: what they do for the heavens, she does for the goods of this world.
A phrase from Virgil's own poetry: a snake lurks in the grass in his third Eclogue.
The angels again. Virgil, a pagan, calls them gods, a usage Dante allows himself elsewhere too.
She has no choice but to keep moving. So many people must have their turn, up and down, that she can never stop.
Cursed and abused. People blame Fortune when their luck turns, though the turning is God's plan and they should thank her.
The angels, the first things God created.
The wheel of Fortune, the familiar medieval image of a wheel that lifts some people up as it carries others down. Dante turns it into a sphere, like those the other angels turn.

quote: every star that was rising when I departed
note: It is past midnight. Virgil left Limbo at dusk on Good Friday. The stars that were rising then have crossed the top of the sky and started down. He tells the time by a sky he can't see.
The water that runs down to feed the Styx. All the rivers of Hell are one stream under different names, and Virgil explains where it comes from in Inferno 14.
The Italian color is perso again, the purple-black of the air in Canto 5.

context: The marsh fills the fifth circle. Dante and Virgil have come down to it without a break, and without a guardian to pass.

note: The wrathful. In life they lashed out at everyone. Here they go on doing it, naked in the mud, with only each other to attack.

quote: beneath the water are people who sigh
note: A second group, hidden under the surface. Who they are is debated. Some take them for the other kind of anger, the kind that is swallowed and smolders. Others take them for the slothful, since Dante's word for their "sluggish smoke" is the word for the sin of sloth.
They refused to be glad in the sunlight, so now they lie in the dark with mud in their mouths. They kept their feelings choked down in life, and can't get even this sentence out whole.
Said with irony. A hymn is a song of praise. This one is a complaint gurgled through mud.
The canto stops short. What the tower is for comes at the start of Canto 8.
